entities.name: Ulugh Beg
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Mīrzā Muhammad Tarāghāy bin Shāhrukh, widely known as Ulugh Beg (1384–1449), was not only a Timurid sultan who ruled Transoxiana from 1447 to 1449 but also an extraordinary astronomer and mathematician whose scientific contributions profoundly influenced the Islamic world and beyond. Grandson of the formidable conqueror Timur, Ulugh Beg inherited a vast, albeit politically volatile, empire, yet he dedicated much of his life to intellectual pursuits, transforming his capital, Samarkand, into a leading center of scientific learning in the 15th century.

Ulugh Beg's most enduring legacy is the construction of the Samarkand Observatory (Ghurkhani Zij) around 1420, a monumental undertaking that featured a massive Fakhri sextant with a radius of 40.4 meters, allowing for unprecedented precision in astronomical observations. Collaborating with brilliant scholars like Jamshid al-Kashi and Qadi Zada al-Rumi, he compiled the 'Zij-i Sultani' (Sultanic Tables) in 1437, a comprehensive star catalogue that listed 1,018 stars with remarkable accuracy, improving upon Ptolemy's Almagest. This work also included tables of planetary movements and trigonometric functions, demonstrating advanced mathematical methods for the era.

Though his reign as sultan was brief and tumultuous, ending tragically with his assassination orchestrated by his own son Abd al-Latif, Ulugh Beg's scientific achievements resonated for centuries. His star catalogue remained a foundational text for astronomers from the Middle East to Europe, notably influencing Nicolaus Copernicus and Tycho Brahe. The meticulous observational data and innovative mathematical techniques developed under his patronage represented a pinnacle of Islamic science, ensuring the transmission of sophisticated astronomical knowledge into the early modern period.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ulugh Beg's astronomical observations and the 'Zij-i Sultani' represented a peak of scientific accuracy in the 15th century, transmitting advanced knowledge that influenced global astronomy for centuries. His work maintained the intellectual momentum of the Islamic Golden Age and provided crucial data for later European scholars.
